title: Chapter 11 — Nightgown
paragraphs: We had lain in bed chatting and napping in short intervals, with Queequeg now and then affectionately throwing his brown tattooed legs over mine and drawing them back. We were so entirely sociable and free and easy together. At last, our confabulations chased away what little nappishness remained in us, and we felt like getting up — though dawn was still some way off.

We grew so wide awake that lying down became tiresome. Little by little we sat up, bedclothes tucked snugly around us, leaning against the headboard with our four knees drawn up close together and our two noses bent over them, as if our kneecaps were warming pans. We felt wonderfully cozy, especially since it was so cold outside — and outside the blankets too, since there was no fire in the room. To truly enjoy bodily warmth, some small part of you must be cold, because no quality in this world exists except by contrast. Nothing exists in itself. If you flatter yourself that you've been comfortable all over for a long time, then you can no longer be said to be comfortable at all. But if, like Queequeg and me in that bed, only the tip of your nose or the crown of your head is slightly chilled, then in your general consciousness you feel most delightfully and unmistakably warm. For this reason, a bedroom should never have a fire — that's one of the luxurious discomforts of the rich. The height of this kind of bliss is having nothing but the blanket between your warmth and the cold outside air. Then you lie like the one warm spark in the heart of an arctic crystal.

We had been sitting hunched like this for some time when all at once I decided to open my eyes. When I'm between sheets, day or night, awake or asleep, I tend to keep my eyes shut to concentrate the snugness of being in bed. Because no person can truly feel their own identity unless their eyes are closed — as if darkness were the proper element of our essence, though light suits our clay better. Opening my eyes and leaving my own pleasant, self-created darkness for the imposed, coarse outer gloom of an unlit midnight, I felt a disagreeable jolt. Nor did I object at all when Queequeg hinted that perhaps we had better light a lamp, since we were wide awake and he badly wanted a few quiet puffs from his tomahawk pipe. I should mention that I'd been dead set against his smoking in bed the night before; yet see how elastic our stiff prejudices become once love starts to bend them. Now I liked nothing better than having Queequeg smoke beside me — even in bed — because he seemed so full of serene, domestic contentment. I no longer worried about the landlord's fire insurance. I was alive only to the condensed, confidential comfort of sharing a pipe and a blanket with a real friend. With our shaggy jackets around our shoulders, we passed the tomahawk pipe back and forth until a blue hanging canopy of smoke slowly gathered above us, glowing in the flame of the newly lit lamp.

Whether it was that this undulating canopy of smoke carried the savage away to far-distant scenes, I don't know, but he now spoke of his native island; and, eager to hear his history, I begged him to go on and tell it. He gladly agreed. Though at the time I understood quite a few of his words only poorly, later disclosures, after I had grown more familiar with his broken phrasing, now allow me to present the whole story, such as it may prove to be, in the mere skeleton I give here.
